messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Interpreting detection probability estimate from gdistsamp
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Interpreting detection probability estimate from gdistsamp
messages.body_plain:
I think I figured it out. The detection function itself is still 100% at the point, but what the bins are showing using getP() is the area weighted detection probability contributing to the overall detection within your truncation distance. In other words, within each bin, the reported p is not particularly meaningful, but when summed, that is the detection probability within your truncation distance at that point.

Thanks all!

Cheers,
-Tyler

My question is: is it correct to make predictions based on this top models? Should I do something additional before obtaining these predictions? Any suggestion is very much appreciated. Thank you all in advance for your time and help.
Best,
Laura

Hi again Geraldine. I received your data. Thanks for sending it.

Due to the unevenness of the sampling within and among primary periods, I have little expectation that the relatively simplistic `formatLong` will construct your `unmarkedFramePCO` object correctly without passing a custom `primaryPeriod` matrix. In your case, that `primaryPeriod` matrix would a 53 x 18*29 matrix identifying the primary period of each secondary sampling event. That doesn't sound like much fun to create...

So I think your best bet is to follow Andy's advise of creating each piece separately and passing them directly to the `unmarkedFramePCO` constructor function.

Best of luck,
Adam

I have to ask:  Why do you need separate estimates of detection probability for each site?  Might there not be available covariates that might explain any differences in detection probabilities among sites?

Jim

Laura,

I encountered this issue myself a couple of weeks ago. You need to add a couple more steps (example code included):

1. Assess model fit for each candidate model using mb.gof.test()

fm2.gof <- mb.gof.test(fm2gof,print.table = TRUE,nsim = 1000,report = TRUE,plot.seasons = TRUE)

2. If any models are significantly (p < 0.05) under-dispersed (c-hat < 1), you don't need to do anything. Just make sure that c-hat in your original AIC is set to 1. If any models are significantly (p < 0.05) over-dispersed (c-hat > 1), you need to record their c-hat values and re-run the entire model set using Q-AIC. Run a separate Q-AIC analysis for each over-dispersed model, setting the Q-AIC c-hat value to that of the model you are focussing on.

QAICc1 <- aictab(cand.mods, second.ord = TRUE, nobs = NULL, sort = TRUE, c.hat = 2.73) #Over-dispersed model 1
QAICc2 <- aictab(cand.mods, second.ord = TRUE, nobs = NULL, sort = TRUE, c.hat = 2.78) #Over-dispersed model 2

3. Based on the QAIC values of the over-dispersed models, re-rank them within your original AIC analysis. They should have moved down a couple of ranks.

4. Remember that you now need to transform your parameter estimates of the over-dispersed models. For each over-dispersed model, multiply the standard errors of β (slope) and ρ (detection, or your parameter of interest) by √ ĉ.

5. You should now have some re-ranked models! Throw them into your AIC table, and just note that some have been ranked using QAIC.

Best,

Sean

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I agree that the stacking method ignores some variability by assuming that measurements from the same site are independent across years. However, it's probably not such a big deal. And: people got away (and still get away all the time) with treating pieces of individual capture histories as independent in the m-array formulation of fitting the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model: I have never heard anybody complain about pseudoreplication there (i.e., that you have to fit a random individual effect). Hence, I would try to argue that stacking is often a reasonable thing to do, because it allows you to very easily fit models with trends across years. Just treat the significance tests with a little caution, since they are likely to be a little too liberal.

Best regards  ---- Marc

Hi Brett,

this is a very good point. To make predictions from a data.frame( ), you need to use a data.frame where the variables are of the same type and use the same coding as your original data set used in the analysis. For instance, in your second example, you reordered the factor level to use LO as the reference level.

As a result, when you create your data set:

> newdat <- data.frame(guild=c("LO", "HI", "SE"))

R uses HI as the reference level as the default contrast coding:

> levels(newdat$guild)
[1] "HI" "LO" "SE"

To ensure that the factors are coded in the same way, it is safer to use:

Hello Jess,

I'm fairly new to this but have had some recent experience.

Firstly, colext models the initial Psi 'state' and then the transitions between each season. With 4 seasons this means you have three transitions S1-S2, S2-S3, S3-S4. The yearly covariates therefore only require three values (one for each transition) but the data input requires four values, so often a dummy value is supplied (NA seems fine??). There are a few posts in this forum about this already by people who actually know what they are talking about, so please refer to them. Your lion data has four values, so the fourth will be ignored (or you can enter in the 4th as NA's).

Your predict values for Psi look good, but your plot uses a ribbon based on predict +/- SE. This is incorrect as you should transform the values into logit space before adding/subtracting SE or CI to a mean, then backtransforming the values. Better yet, use the predicted "lower" and "upper" values which should be the default 95% confidence limits.

Predicting gamma and epsilon requires a value for each of the transitions - in this case three. It should be fairly straight forward for a linear value - just ensure they are of type "numeric" (rather than factor or character).

for starters, try:
ndlion <- data.frame(lion=c(0.12,0.12,0.12))
predict.col<- predict(ge.water_lion, type="col", newdata=ndlion, appendData=TRUE)

If this works then you should be able to make a 'ndlion' dataframe exploring the different combinations of lion values you have or expect to have and plot the different scenarios.

I hope this works, I hope this is correct and I hope it has helped.

Cheers,
Al

However, I do think that adjustments of some kind are warranted because predictions from this models are not at all reasonable (too high).

This isn't unexpected. AIC = -2 Log Like +2K; QAIC = 2 Log Like/c-hat +2K, so the contribution of the likelihood is being penalized. Larger sample size generally means a larger log-likelihood, so ranking differences between AIC and QAIC with c-hat held constant tend to be larger for larger sample sizes. I don't know of any justification for not making a correction for overdispersion.

> 2) About pos-hoc adjustments. Other than the SE, what other parameters should I adjust multiplying by c-hat?

It's suggested to adjust every standard error by sqrt(c-hat), but not the parameter estimates themselves.

Hi folks

I'm trying to compare results from fitting a hierarchical distance sampling model with the unmarked package and a Bayesian implementation using JAGS.  I successfully fit a basic single-occasion HDS model with a half-normal detection function and negative binomial abundance model using the gdistsamp function in unmarked. However, when I fitted a Bayesian version in JAGS, I ran into trouble with estimating sigma for the detection function. Essentially, the posterior continually pushed up against the upper bound of the uniform prior as I incrementally increased that bound which basically caused detection to be 1 at all feasible distances and the abundance estimates to equal the raw counts. My guess is that I have some inherent mis-specification in my JAGS model statement that I am unable to see. Perhaps someone else out there can spot the problem. My test is based on real data that I would be willing to share offline if necessary. In short, the data contains too many transects with zero counts to fit a Poisson abundance model, hence the negative binomial. The transect half-width is 300 m and distance bins are 50 m. Perfect detection can safely be assumed at distance 0. The detection parameter estimates from the unmarked analysis do result in a detection function that aligns with field expectations and similar studies on the same taxon. Note that I have already tried using estimates from the unmarked analysis as starting values for the JAGS analysis. No bueno. Any insights would be greatly appreciated. Below is the JAGS model statement and calls to the requisite unmarked functions to fit the likelihood version.

Cheers!
Jared

cat("
    model{
        ## priors
        beta0 ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
        r ~ dunif(0,upperr)
        sigma ~ dunif(0,500)
        ## derive psi
        psi <- sum(Ng[])/(ngroups+nz)
        ## detection model
        for(i in 1:(ngroups+nz)){
            z[i] ~ dbern(psi) # data augmentation model
            bindist[i] ~ dcat(pi[]) # distance distribution (prior)
            mu.p[i] <- z[i]*exp(-bindist[i]*bindist[i]/(2*sigma*sigma)) # detection function
            y[i] ~ dbern(mu.p[i])
            transect[i] ~ dcat(transect.probs[1:ntransects]) # multinomial for transect membership
        }
        ##
        for(s in 1:ntransects){
            ## population model
            Ng[s] ~ dnegbin(p[s],r) # transect-level abundance
            log(mu.nb[s]) <- beta0
            p[s] <- r/(mu.nb[s] + r)
            transect.probs[s] <- Ng[s]/sum(Ng[]) # probability vector for multinomial
        }
        ##
        ## derived quantities
        G <- sum(z[]) # total population abundance across transects
    }
    ",fill=TRUE, file="model0.jags")
